title: Kaddish for the teachers
hook: a Kaddish praying for teachers, their students and their students' students

segments.voice: Yesterday, korbanot, the offerings read in place of the altar. Your line was words instead of offerings. Did you say the words to the person they belonged to? Today, the prayer that closes that section. Day five hundred fifty-two.

Every teacher had a teacher. The fourth-grade teacher who read aloud with all the voices learned it from someone. So did the coach, and the grandmother at the kitchen table. And who taught them? Somewhere back along that line is a stranger whose patience is still being passed along, though nobody remembers their name. Jewish prayer has a moment set aside for that whole invisible line. It comes right after a few minutes of study, and it's one of the forms of the Kaddish.
screen: `EVERY TEACHER HAD A TEACHER.` → `AND WHO TAUGHT THEM?` → `AN INVISIBLE LINE.`

segments.voice: The Kaddish is often thought of as the mourner's prayer. In fact it comes in several forms, and all of them share a core, in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in the age of the Talmud: may God's great name be made great and holy in the world. The congregation answers: may God's great name be blessed forever. The Kaddish d'Rabbanan, the Kaddish of the rabbis, is said after a group has studied rabbinic teaching together. In the morning service it comes at the end of the readings you heard about yesterday. And it adds one paragraph that no other Kaddish has. It asks for blessing on Israel, and on the teachers, and on their students, and on all their students' students, and on everyone who studies Torah, here and in every place. It asks for peace, grace, kindness and compassion, long life, enough to live on, and help from heaven. Notice how far it reaches. Not just my teacher. The teachers, the students, the students of the students, spreading out across places and generations. Like every Kaddish, it's said only with a minyan, the quorum for communal prayer, and often mourners lead it. The Talmud, in tractate Sotah, says the world is held up by the response to the Kaddish said after study. Learning isn't treated as private. It ends with a prayer for everyone who carried it to you, and everyone you'll carry it to.
screen: `KADDISH: MAY THE NAME BE HALLOWED.` · `SAID AFTER STUDYING TOGETHER.` · `TEACHERS, STUDENTS, THEIR STUDENTS.` · `ONLY WITH A MINYAN.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a teacher in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the face of one teacher who mattered to you, living or gone. Remember one thing they said or did that stayed. Then widen the picture: their teacher, behind them, and behind that one, a line going back further than you can see. Then look forward: the people you've taught, even a little, a child, a friend, a coworker. If you pray, you can ask God's peace for the whole line. If not, simply wish it to them. The bell holds the time.
Kaddish d'Rabbanan. The Kaddish of the rabbis, said after study, with a paragraph for teachers and their students' students.
Your line: pray for the teachers. Today, send a short thank you to one teacher, or tell someone else about them if you can't reach them anymore. Day five hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Kaddish d'Rabbanan is said in a minyan after a passage of rabbinic study, including in the morning service after the readings on the offerings; mourners often lead it, and the congregation answers.

original.note: Aramaic: the Kaddish of the rabbis. kaddish means holy, sanctified.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for the dead.
what it means: after study, a prayer for everyone who carried the teaching, and everyone it will reach.
what a scholar hears: the al Yisrael paragraph is unique to this Kaddish; Sotah 49a says the world stands on the yehei shemei rabba said after aggadic study.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): replaced the banned 'Think of' hook opener; 'Most people know the Kaddish as' softened to 'often thought of as'; 'ten adults' (a count, and practice differs) now 'the quorum for communal prayer' in voice and match.
Kaddish core and the al Yisrael paragraph paraphrased from the standard siddur; confirm list of requests (peace, grace, kindness, compassion, long life, ample sustenance, salvation).
Sotah 49a: the world endures on the kedushah d'sidra and yehei shemei rabba of aggadah; confirm the paraphrase.
Placement in the morning service after Rabbi Yishmael's thirteen principles (end of the korbanot section) in Ashkenazi rites; confirm, and note Sephardi differences.
'Ten adults': traditional Orthodox practice counts ten men; many non-Orthodox communities count women. Wording kept neutral; confirm.
